examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a medical necessity that reduces the risk of SIDS and is affordable, because they are willing to pay a premium for a product that addresses a serious health concern.
theories.T2: Parents of low‑birth‑weight infants will adopt a home‑use infant warmer if they perceive it as a convenient, affordable way to monitor their baby’s temperature and health at home, because they value time‑saving and ease of use, and are willing to pay a price that reflects the convenience.

arguments.name: Two-arm refundable-deposit pre-order test: clinician-endorsed thermal-safety kit vs night-check relief bundle
arguments.method: Target customers: US parents of newborns in the months after birth — the market where Embrace already sells direct at $85 (embrace-cnbc-price). Proposed 5,000 qualified visitors, with a screening question flagging parents of pre-term or low-birth-weight babies so both arms compare within that group. Treatment: Clinical thermal-safety kit: the warming device plus a written thermal-safety protocol with named paediatrician endorsement, described for pre-term and low-birth-weight babies at home. $199 with a $50 refundable deposit; layout, imagery and copy length identical to the control. Control: Night-check relief bundle: the same device plus a temperature-alert monitor, described as cutting night-time checking and clinic trips. Same $199 price, same $50 refundable deposit, same layout and copy length; only the described attribute and use case differ.
arguments.sample: Traffic from the existing Little Lotus/Embrace site plus a modest paid campaign to new-parent and preemie forums and newsletters, about €10,000 of the budget in ad spend. Visitors are randomly assigned to one of the two pages; a completed $50 refundable deposit is the participation act. Proposed total: 5,000 qualified visitors over 8 weeks.
arguments.measure: Refundable $50 deposits per 1,000 qualified visitors in each arm, plus the share of depositors who report a pre-term or low-birth-weight baby, and refunds/cancellations by week 10. Deposits are real money and refundable, so they measure commitment better than stated intent but still over-state final purchase.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The clinician-endorsed thermal-safety kit out-converts the monitor bundle by at least 30%, at least 60% of all depositors are parents of pre-term or low-birth-weight babies, and conversion holds at the $199 price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The monitor bundle out-converts the thermal-safety kit by at least 30%, and depositors look like general new parents, with the pre-term/low-birth-weight share below 40% of depositors.

arguments.decision_rule: Stop if total deposits across both arms fall below 40 from 5,000 qualified visitors (0.8%). T1 supported if the clinical kit converts at least 1.3x the monitor arm and LBW/pre-term depositors are at least 60%. T2 supported if the monitor arm converts at least 1.3x and LBW share is below 40%. If deposits reach 40 but arms are within 30% of each other, cause undetermined and no product line. Below 40: drop the consumer proposition, stay with B2B (option 3). T1 pattern: fund a bounded 8-10 week regional pilot of ~100 clinical kits via clinician referral at discharge, measuring sell-through. T2 pattern: run a 12-week trial of the bundle with one baby-retail partner rather than new distribution. Undetermined: no build; use the remainder on one partner-channel trial to test whether channel, not mechanism, is the blocker.

justification.learned: Consumers are reachable: "Little Lotus products are available for sale on the company website, and swaddles have recently decreased in price from $98 to $85" (embrace-cnbc-price) — a $85 direct-to-consumer US swaddle, not a warmer. The warmer is clinical: "the Embrace® Nest was launched in 2011 in India, where it is widely used" (embrace-smg-launch), built for "settings where conventional incubators could be difficult to obtain" (embrace-ee-origin). Warmth worry is anecdote (embrace-yahoo-origin); the SIDS link is only a company claim (embrace-her-sids). Investors need commercial scale (embrace-gsb-investors). No source shows consumer demand, price response or margin: demand unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether parents commit real money, and whether the cause is medical necessity (T1) or night-check relief (T2): nothing measures willingness to pay for a home warmer, only the $85 swaddle anchor (embrace-cnbc-price). Unknown whether a SIDS/medical framing for a home device is legally usable in 2016 — a magazine claim (embrace-her-sids) is not clearance, so T1's mechanism could be blocked. Scale and margin unknown. Deposits, visitor counts and €20,000 are proposed parameters, not market facts.
justification.why_next: A deposit test separates T1 from T2: each names a different cause, predicting different winners and buyer mix (embrace-cnbc-price, embrace-yahoo-origin, embrace-her-sids, embrace-ee-origin). T1: buyers are parents of pre-term/low-birth-weight babies seeking medical risk reduction, so the clinician-endorsed thermal-safety kit out-converts and depositors concentrate among LBW parents. T2: buyers are any exhausted new parents buying night-check relief, so the monitor bundle wins and depositors resemble general new parents. Arms share price, layout, channel and creative; random assignment and depositor mix address creative, targeting and novelty alternatives. Fits €20,000 and 12 weeks.

examples.question: It is late 2014. Should Perrigo develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its over-the-counter medicine development and manufacturing? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Perrigo consumer brand if they perceive it as a premium, quality product that differentiates from generic alternatives, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated Perrigo consumer brand if they perceive it as a convenient, convenient-to-buy product that is readily available in pharmacies and retail outlets, leading to higher purchase frequency and lower price sensitivity.

arguments.reason: Blocked by feasibility and conflict: Perrigo makes the store brands of the retailers who would have to stock any Perrigo brand (perrigo-bar-retailers, perrigo-bar-penetration); its own Good Sense stayed a small share of sales (perrigo-fu-goodsense). A test needs a registered SKU, pack and retailer agreement — beyond €20,000/12 weeks — and cannot separate T1 from T2, which differ only in premium size.

justification.learned: Perrigo's only consumer brand found, Good Sense, is small: such products "account for only a small percentage of sales" (perrigo-fu-goodsense), but "If the price difference was too dramatic... the consumer became suspicious of the Perrigo brand and turned to the national brand" (perrigo-fu-suspicious). Its proven model is making retailer store brands, "Big Dollar Profits and Margin for Retailers" (perrigo-bar-retailers), cetirizine at "48% penetration" (perrigo-bar-penetration). Nov 2014: €3.6bn for Omega Pharma's branded OTCs sold through "an extensive network of pharmacies" (perrigo-ppr-omega, perrigo-pml-gsk, perrigo-ppr-pharmacies). No source measures demand for a Perrigo brand.
justification.uncertain: Demand for a Perrigo-branded OTC, and its cause, is unmeasured: evidence is company claims plus one secondhand observation, not consumer behaviour (perrigo-fu-suspicious). T1 and T2 are not separated — both assume lower price sensitivity at a premium, differing only in premium size (20% vs 10%). Unknown: whether retailers would stock a brand competing with their own store brands, and Omega's per-market economics, as "$1.6 billion of revenue" is a company claim (perrigo-ppr-omega).
justification.why_next: I decline to test: the binding constraint is channel access, not consumer motivation, and it lies outside what €20,000 and 12 weeks can buy. Perrigo earns from the retailers whose store brands it makes (perrigo-bar-retailers, perrigo-bar-penetration); a branded proposition needs shelf space from those same customers plus a registered SKU, with no retailer-cooperation evidence in the dossier. An affordable test cannot separate T1 from T2, whose predictions differ only in premium size, nor show repeat purchase. Acting beats waiting: the brand question is being answered at €3.6bn scale by Omega's branded OTCs and pharmacy network (perrigo-ppr-omega, perrigo-pml-gsk, perrigo-ppr-pharmacies).

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.name: Two-arm deposit pilot: custom-moulded plugs for musicians vs. noise-sensitive sleepers
arguments.method: Target customers: Semi-professional and gigging musicians in one French metro area, and noise-sensitive adults (light sleepers and shift workers) in the same area. Both are individual payers, which is the group the dossier never shows Cotral reaching. Treatment: Musician arm: a custom-moulded pair with Cotral's frequency-specific filters offered at €180 with a €30 deposit, presented as preserving musical sound while lowering level, with free impressions taken at a partner audiology site. Same price, deposit and fitting procedure as the other arm; only segment and positioning differ. Control: Sleeper arm: the same custom-moulded pair at the same €180 with the same €30 deposit and the same fitting procedure, presented as reducing night-time noise disruption, with no medical or curative claim. Identical leaflet layout, offer window and fulfiller.
arguments.sample: 60 qualified prospects per arm (120 total, proposed): musicians recruited through three rehearsal studios/music shops and two music-school mailing lists, sleepers through two pharmacies and two sleep-interest community groups, all in one metro area. Each gets the same one-page offer and a 21-day window.
arguments.measure: Number of paid €30 deposits per arm within 21 days, and how many deposit-payers actually attend the fitting; deposit money is real and refundable only if Cotral cannot deliver. Price and deposit are proposed parameters, not market facts.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Musicians convert at ≥6 of 60 (10%) while sleepers convert at ≤3 of 60 (5% or less), because sound preservation is the value driver worth a premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sleepers convert at ≥6 of 60 while musicians convert at ≤3 of 60, because the perceived health benefit, not sound quality, is what people pay for.

arguments.decision_rule: The screen is 6 deposits out of 60 (about 10%) per arm against 3 out of 60 (5%) in the other; anything in between is a null result. Thresholds are proposed for a small partner pilot, not statistically precise. One arm ≥6 and the other ≤3: run a six-month single-segment pilot with one fitting partner, capped at the same order of spend, before any product-line decision. Both arms ≤3: stop the consumer idea and keep the employer-paid B2B focus. Both arms ≥6: hold the segment question open and run one price variant (€240) in both arms before choosing. Deposits taken but fittings unattended in over half the cases: treat as failure of the route, not of demand.

justification.learned: Capability and channel are shown; demand is not. Cotral Lab is "the world's No.1 manufacturer of custom-molded hearing protection" whose products "will continue to be distributed primarily through direct channels to end-user companies" (ctl-channel); impressions are "taken directly on-site" for employees (ctl-onsite), and IT1 addresses employees (ctl-it1) — an employer-paid B2B route with no evidence of a consumer paying. Musician capability exists (ctl-filter), but one independent study undercuts T1: appreciation "mainly depended on comfort and looks" (bockstael-2015-looks), and an adjustable-fidelity plug already exists (minuendo-claim). Sleep demand is unknown (T2).
justification.uncertain: No source shows individual willingness to pay, a French consumer price for custom moulds, repeat use or unit economics; Cotral's financials are not public. T2's "medical-grade" framing raises a regulatory question I have no source for. Whether Cotral would join a pilot, or a partner would take impressions, is unverified — the company has not been contacted. One competitor result (etymotic-er20xs) went unread. The 6-of-60 threshold is a coarse proposed screen.
justification.why_next: The deposit pilot separates T1 from T2 because both arms get identical product, €180 price, €30 deposit and fulfilment, differing only in segment and positioning: T1 predicts musicians commit at a premium, T2 predicts noise-sensitive sleepers do. Real money and a live fitting test payer willingness, not stated intent; the B2B-only route in ctl-channel and ctl-onsite is why the offer runs through a borrowed fitting partner, and ctl-filter makes the attribute real. It stays a partner trial, not a product line, because no source shows consumer demand to size against (bockstael-2015-looks and minuendo-claim leave the sound-quality mechanism contested).

arguments.name: Two-price pre-order deposit test for a ready-to-use biological control kit, Netherlands
arguments.method: Target customers: Dutch home gardeners with a vegetable plot, allotment or small greenhouse who already buy garden inputs such as seeds, compost and pest products; they are reached online, the one channel where price can be varied cleanly. Treatment: High-price cell: an identical kit at 34.95 EUR for the season, same page, photos, kit contents, copy and delivery terms as the control; only price differs. A refundable 5 EUR deposit by card secures the kit for spring delivery. Control: Low-price cell: the same kit at 19.95 EUR, same page, creative, contents and delivery terms, same refundable 5 EUR deposit by card; both cells run simultaneously with randomised ad delivery so audience mix is comparable.
arguments.sample: About 12000 to 16000 Dutch home gardeners brought to the offer page by paid social and search ads aimed at allotment and vegetable-garden interests, split by random assignment into two equal price cells with identical ads and audience settings.
arguments.measure: Deposit conversion per cell: paid deposits divided by unique visitors to the offer page, plus deposits refunded within four weeks. Both are observed purchasing behaviour with real money at stake; the deposit is small, so the rate is a ceiling on demand, not a forecast.

arguments.method: Target customers: US adults who cut their own or a household member's hair at least monthly; Andis's home line is USD-priced and the euro budget is converted in the cost line. Treatment: Two premium arms at the same proposed $89 price, same page layout, same $10 refundable deposit ask, differing only in real product configuration: (A) professional-precision - pro-grade blade set, higher-torque motor, barber-designed styling guide; (B) convenience - cordless, quick-swap blades, compact body, 5-minute quick-guide. $89 is proposed, about 50% above the observed $59.99 tier. arguments.sample: 600 US adults (200 per arm) recruited through one online consumer panel, screened as monthly home haircutters; each is randomly assigned one of the three offer pages, so arms are comparable.

examples.question: It is mid-2014. Should ResMed develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its non-contact sleep-sensing technology and sleep-medicine expertise? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Individuals with sleep apnoea will adopt a home sleep test device if they perceive it as convenient and accurate, and if they are willing to pay a premium for non-contact technology that avoids the need for clinic visits.
theories.T2: Insurance companies will cover home sleep tests if they are validated against polysomnography and demonstrate clinical efficacy, leading consumers to adopt home testing because they avoid clinic visits and reduce out-of-pocket costs.

arguments.name: Deposit-paid pre-order test: self-pay $149.99 vs payer-billed $30 co-pay for a non-contact home sleep assessment, US
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 30-60 who report snoring, witnessed breathing pauses or daytime sleepiness and have had no sleep study in the past 12 months. They are reached by identical keyword and interest ad sets pointing to the same page; target of about 2,500 qualified visitors per arm over 8 weeks (proposed parameter, not a market estimate). Treatment: Payer-billed route: same device and same page, but the offer is a $30 patient co-pay with the balance billed to the buyer's insurer through a partner home-health dealer after a short sleep-symptom questionnaire and a coverage eligibility check; a $25 refundable deposit reserves the unit. Control: Self-pay route: same device, same page, same questionnaire and same $25 refundable deposit, but a total out-of-pocket price of $149.99 with no third-party payment. Only the price and who pays differ between arms.
arguments.sample: Adults are recruited through online search and social advertising aimed at sleep-apnoea symptom terms, plus a screened panel of self-reported snorers, with the same creative and budget split evenly; about 2,500 qualified visitors per arm and roughly 100-150 depositors in total expected if conversion is in the predicted range (all figures proposed).
arguments.measure: Primary measure is the share of qualified visitors per arm who place a paid, refundable $25 deposit within the 8-week advertising window. Secondary measures are the share of depositors who complete full payment or confirmed eligibility within 4 weeks of depositing, and the refund rate. Deposits are real money, but they are refundable, so they establish commitment short of a completed sale.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Self-pay conversion is material and not lower than the co-pay arm: expect at least 3% of qualified visitors in the $149.99 self-pay arm to deposit, with the two arms within about 2 percentage points of each other. If convenience and non-contact accuracy are what people buy, out-of-pocket cost is not the gate.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Self-pay conversion collapses: expect under 1% of qualified visitors in the $149.99 self-pay arm to deposit, while the $30 co-pay arm reaches at least 3%. If third-party payment is what unlocks adoption, removing the cost barrier should move commitment by several-fold under otherwise identical presentation.

arguments.decision_rule: Required two-sided gap of at least 2 percentage points. T1 supported if self-pay converts at or above 3% and is within 2pp of co-pay. T2 supported if self-pay converts below 1% while co-pay is at or above 3% (gap ≥2pp). If both arms fall between 1% and 3%, both below 1%, or co-pay stays below 3%, neither theory is supported and the result counts against both. If T1: bounded direct-sales pilot for one use case (adults suspecting sleep apnoea), a few thousand units with one retail or web partner, revisited only after sell-through data. If T2: stop the direct consumer channel; run a partner trial with one home-health dealer and one payer to establish coverage, treating the proposition as payer-funded. If neither: stop the consumer proposition and keep the dealer and clinic business (resmed-10k-clinics, resmed-10k-dealer).

No source shows an individual buying directly, so consumer demand is unknown. Accuracy is documented, not demand: "overall per-subject accuracy was 78%, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.38" (resmed-pm-dechazal2011); "accurate, touch-free" is a company claim (resmed-pr-biancamed). The $149.99 price (resmed-pr-splus) is dated October 2014, after the decision, and shows a price, not purchases. T1 and T2 both survive.

examples.question: It is March 2016. Should Embrace Innovations develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its infant-warming technology? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants in low-resource settings will adopt a home infant warmer if it is priced below $100 and marketed as a life-saving medical device that reduces the risk of SIDS.
theories.T2: Parents of premature and low-birth-weight infants will adopt a home infant warmer if it is marketed as a fashion accessory and sold through trendy consumer channels, because they view infant care as a status symbol and are willing to pay a premium for design and brand.

arguments.name: Refundable-deposit pre-order test: home warming kit at $89 vs $149
arguments.method: Target customers: Parents in the United States who are expecting a baby or have a newborn born early (preterm/NICU graduates), the group T1 says has the acute medical need and T2 says buys premium baby goods. This is a proposed segment, reachable through Embrace's existing Little Lotus direct channel and preterm-parent communities. Treatment: Identical landing page for the same home warming kit for babies born early, with the same images, copy and delivery terms, showing a price of $149 and a $20 refundable reservation deposit. Only the price differs from control; no fashion or status language is added, so the price itself is the variable. Control: Same page in every respect — same product, copy, images, delivery terms, $20 refundable deposit — but priced at $89, inside the band at which Little Lotus swaddles actually sell ($85–98 per embrace-cnbc-price).
arguments.sample: About 5,000 unique US visitors, roughly 2,500 per arm, randomly assigned at page load: paid social ads (identical creative across arms) targeted at parents of premature infants and NICU groups, plus Embrace's existing Little Lotus email list. Two weeks of build, eight weeks live, two weeks for refunds and analysis, inside the 12-week limit.
arguments.measure: Real commitment, not stated intent: share of visitors who place a $20 refundable deposit, deposits per arm, share of depositors who confirm a preterm/NICU birth, and cancellation/refund rate at eight weeks. Deposits are refundable, so this is a reservation commitment, not a completed sale — it shows willingness to act and to pay a given price, not lifetime demand.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The $89 arm converts at 2.0% or more of visitors and at least double the $149 arm, because price-sensitive parents buying on medical necessity are deterred by a $60 higher price for the same product.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The $149 arm converts at 1.5% or more and no lower than 0.8x the $89 arm, because buyers purchasing for status and perceived quality treat a higher price as a signal rather than a barrier, even with identical presentation.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed thresholds, not market facts: 2.0% deposit rate at $89, 1.5% at $149, and a 2x ratio between arms. With ~2,500 visitors per arm these are decision rules, not precise estimates; small absolute counts (tens of deposits) mean I treat results as directional and claim no statistical power. $89 at 2.0%+ and 2x $149: T1 favoured — fund a 300-kit pilot via the Little Lotus channel, reviewed after six months. $149 at 1.5%+ and 0.8x+ of $89: T2 mechanism survives — one premium design-edition prototype trialled with one retail partner for 12 weeks, no product line. Both arms under 1.0%: stop the consumer proposition, keep B2B. $89 between 1.0% and 2.0% and still 2x: only a 150-unit partner-funded production test, otherwise stop. Anything else unproven: stop unless a partner funds.

justification.learned: Embrace already reaches individual buyers: Little Lotus swaddles 'are available for sale on the company website, and swaddles have recently decreased in price from $98 to $85' (embrace-cnbc-price, 2016-02-22) — a direct channel under price pressure, not premium. The warmer is clinical in origin (embrace-ee-origin) and 'the Embrace® Nest was launched in 2011 in India, where it is widely used' (embrace-smg-launch) — institutional, not proof parents buy. No revenue, units or consumer purchases appear anywhere: demand unknown. embrace-gsb-investors (2012) warns investors need attractive segments. Beliefs: T1 uncertain, T2 unlikely (the price cut cuts against premium status pricing).
justification.uncertain: Whether any parent commits money for home warming, and at what price. No source shows a consumer warmer purchase, revenue, or a home-use regulatory position (no FDA/CE source is in the dossier), and none sizes the preterm/LBW consumer segment. Reaching NICU parents affordably is unproven. A price-only design barely probes T2's status mechanism — a stated limit, not a finding.
justification.why_next: Declining is wrong: 0 searches left, no blocking constraint in state (embrace-cnbc-price shows Embrace already sells direct at $85–98), and no source resolves whether individuals pay for warming. The test separates T1 from T2 because their mechanisms imply opposite price reactions with identical presentation: T1 (embrace-ee-origin, embrace-smg-launch) predicts commitment collapses at a premium; T2 (no supporting source, contradicted in direction by the price cut) predicts a higher price does not deter status buyers. embrace-gsb-investors keeps every branch bounded.

theories.T1: Consumers will adopt Illumina’s direct‑to‑consumer genetic testing because they view it as a health‑management tool that provides actionable insights, leading them to purchase at‑home kits.
theories.T2: Consumers will adopt Illumina’s direct‑to‑consumer genetic testing because they seek ancestry and heritage insights, leading them to purchase at‑home kits.

arguments.name: Two-cell refundable-deposit pre-order test: health/carrier report vs ancestry report at an identical $99 price
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults aged 25-55 who bought something online in the past 12 months in health/wellness or in family history/genealogy. They are the buyers either theory names, not existing Illumina lab customers. Treatment: A pre-order page for a 'Health & Carrier Screen' report: what the report shows (inherited carrier status for a fixed list of conditions), price $99, a $25 refundable deposit to reserve a kit, delivery promised in about 6 months. Layout, copy length, images, terms, refund policy and checkout are held identical to the control. Control: The same page at the same $99 price and same $25 refundable deposit, with only the report content changed to 'Ancestry & Heritage' (regional composition and relative matching). Brand, images, terms, refund policy and checkout are unchanged, so the only difference is which benefit the product claims to deliver.
arguments.sample: 400 adults through a commercial online panel, randomised within panel to about 200 per cell, with quotas for age, sex and region. Screening asks only about recent online purchases in health or genealogy, never which report a person prefers. These are proposed parameters, not market facts.
arguments.measure: Primary: share of exposed panellists who actually pay the $25 refundable deposit within 14 days, per cell, with card payment captured (real commitment, not stated intent). Secondary: refund requests within 14 days, which bound how firm the commitment is. Stated interest is recorded but is not used for the decision.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health cell about 12% paid deposits versus about 5% for ancestry (at least 1.5x), because buyers are paying to act on carrier risk and health framing carries the value at the same price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Ancestry cell about 14% paid deposits versus about 6% for health (at least 1.5x), because buyers are paying for identity and family curiosity, and a health framing adds regulatory friction without adding that value.

arguments.decision_rule: The winning cell must reach at least 8% paid deposits (8% of 200 = 16 deposits) AND at least 1.5x the other cell. Under 4% in both cells means no consumer demand signal at this price. Health wins (>=8%, >=1.5x): 6-month partner-run pilot of a carrier-screen proposition through a clinical/lab partner. Ancestry wins (>=8%, >=1.5x): 6-month partner pilot of an ancestry kit with Illumina supplying sequencing and arrays. Both under 4%: stop consumer investment and stay in B2B. Both >=8% and within 1.5x: no further testing; choose by capability and regulatory cost (carrier screening exempt from premarket review, illumina-ajmc-bloom) and run one partner pilot.

T1 says a deposit is bought by actionable health management; T2 says it is bought by identity/family curiosity. Under identical price, brand, layout and checkout, and with only the report content changed, the two mechanisms predict opposite relative paid-deposit rates, so one 10-week, EUR 18,000 two-cell test separates T1 from T2 using real money rather than stated intent. Each outcome leads only to a bounded partner pilot or to stopping, never to building a product line; the test does not settle cost of delivery, repeat use or regulatory clearance, which remain for the pilot.

examples.question: Should Cotral Lab develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?

theories.T1: Professional musicians will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a performanceenhancing tool that preserves sound quality while blocking noise, because they value accurate sound and are willing to pay a premium for a product that does not compromise their craft.
theories.T2: Sleep aid users will adopt custom-moulded hearing protection if it is marketed as a medical-grade solution that reduces sleep disruption caused by background noise, because they seek a product that addresses a specific health concern and are willing to pay for a solution that improves sleep quality.

arguments.name: Paid-deposit pilot: musicians vs noise-disturbed sleepers, identical offer mechanics
arguments.method: Target customers: Two groups of individual French buyers from one pool: adults playing an instrument or amplified music at least weekly (T1), and adults whose sleep is regularly disturbed by noise (T2); current Cotral customers and custom-mould owners excluded. Treatment: Musician cell (T1): 100 qualified prospects see one custom-moulded music plug at €149, framed as keeping sound clear while cutting level, with a neutral mention that generic hi-fi plugs cost around €25 (minuendo-claim); they can place a €30 refundable deposit for an impression appointment. Control: Sleeper cell (T2): 100 qualified prospects get the identical product, €149 price, generic-alternative mention and €30 refundable deposit mechanics, with quiet-night wording instead. Same screener, venue, staff and weeks; only segment and wording differ.
arguments.sample: A paid online panel plus local ads in one metro area near Cotral's Normandy base (estimate: Rouen, given the 'Suisse-Normande' base in ctl-filter), with two screening questions to fill 100 musicians and 100 noise-disturbed sleepers over 8 weeks. Identical invitation, incentive and follow-up for both cells.
arguments.measure: Primary: number of €30 refundable deposits per 100 qualified recruits in each cell by week 8 — a real commitment, not stated intent. Secondary: share who attend the impression appointment and pay the remaining €119, and how many say they bought a €25 generic plug instead.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Musicians reach at least 8 paid deposits per 100 qualified and at least double the sleeper rate, because audible clarity during performance is worth a €149 custom mould and generic plugs muffle it; sleepers, lacking that craft motive, stay under 4 per 100.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sleepers reach at least 8 paid deposits per 100 and at least double the musician rate, because noise-broken sleep is a health problem with no adequate cheap fix; musicians stay under 4 per 100 because adjustable hi-fi plugs (Minuendo claims 7–25 dB, minuendo-claim) already give them clarity at retail prices.

arguments.decision_rule: At week 8: musicians ≥8 deposits per 100 and ≥2× the sleeper rate → run the musician pilot. Sleepers ≥8 per 100 and ≥2× the musician rate → run the sleep pilot. Both arms under 4 per 100, or the leading arm under 2× the other → stop consumer work. These are proposed judgment thresholds, not statistical-power claims; with roughly 8 events per arm the result is directional, so show-up and full-payment rates are read alongside it. Musician-led → bounded 100-pair musician pilot with one music-retail or rehearsal-studio partner, capped at an estimated €50k over 6 months. Sleeper-led → bounded 100-pair pilot through one hearing-care or pharmacy partner, only after a legal check on sleep/medical claims. Flat → no consumer proposition now; the €20k is spent, Cotral keeps selling custom moulds through employer channels (ctl-channel) and revisits only if a distributor brings consumer reach.

justification.learned: Cotral Lab is the 'world's No.1 manufacturer of custom-molded hearing protection', now owned by PPE distributor Groupe RG, with products 'distributed primarily through direct channels to end-user companies' (ctl-deal, ctl-channel). The dossier shows a B2B employer route only: no consumer price, channel or purchase. Capability is documented — in-house frequency filters (ctl-filter), 3D printing since 2010 (ctl-3d), on-site impressions (ctl-onsite), Bluetooth IT1 (ctl-it1) — but capability is not demand. Independent musician work found appreciation 'mainly depended on comfort and looks, while differences in sound quality were less noticeable' (bockstael-2015-looks), cutting against T1.
justification.uncertain: Whether any individual buyer would pay a custom-moulded premium: every Cotral source is a company assertion, with no consumer price, conversion or repeat purchase. T1's sound-clarity premium (ctl-filter, minuendo-claim) is undercut by bockstael-2015-looks, where comfort and looks dominated. T2 rests on capability only (ctl-filter, ctl-onsite), no sleep-demand data; no source says if a sleep claim is regulated in France. Consumer reach without a retail partner is unresolved (ctl-channel).
justification.why_next: T1 and T2 name different customer groups, so the open question is which group commits money under identical mechanics. A €30 refundable deposit toward a €149 pair offered to 100 qualified musicians (T1) and 100 qualified noise-disturbed sleepers (T2) through the same screener, venue, staff and weeks measures real commitment: T1 predicts musicians commit at ≥2× sleepers, T2 the reverse, and a flat result says keep the B2B custom-moulded focus (ctl-channel) rather than build a consumer line. bockstael-2015-looks predicts weak musician conversion, so a null is informative. Confound: the groups differ in income; identical recruitment reduces but does not remove it.

arguments.name: Musician vs Sleep Aid Purchase Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a musician-focused proposition (sound-quality preservation) or a sleep-aid proposition (sleep-disruption reduction). Participants indicate willingness to purchase at a €X price point (e.g., €20 for musician, €25 for sleep aid).
arguments.sample: 400 adults recruited via panel, balanced between musicians and sleep aid users, stratified by age and gender to reflect target segments.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness-to-pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Musicians exposed to the musician proposition will show higher purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than sleep aid exposure.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sleep aid users exposed to the sleep aid proposition will show higher purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than musician exposure.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness-to-pay for the musician proposition exceeds the average willingness-to-pay for the sleep aid proposition by ≥€5, proceed with musician-focused proposition. If the difference is <€5, proceed with sleep-aid focus. A

examples.question: Should Andis develop a further differentiated proposition for people who cut hair at home, beyond its existing at-home range, or concentrate on professional barbers and groomers? What evidence would justify either choice?

theories.T1: Home users will adopt a differentiated at-home proposition if they perceive it as a premium, professional-quality experience that builds confidence and reduces salon visits.
theories.T2: Home users will adopt a differentiated at-home proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, time-saving solution that reduces the need for salon visits.

sources_read.andis-1997-home-kits: unknown (International Directory of Company Histories, Volume 85)

arguments.name: US paid pre-order test: professional-grade kit vs ten-minute bundle at the same $89 price
arguments.method: Target customers: US adults who already cut hair at home for themselves or a household member with clippers, the DIYer group Andis already reaches with kits at $24.99-$59.99 (andis-athome-prices). US market, priced in USD as in the sources. Treatment: Landing page for a $89 'Professional Grade' home kit: pro-style blade and motor described, metal guard set, 'the clipper barbers use' claim, no time-saving copy. Same layout, photography and price as the control; the only purchase action is a $20 refundable deposit toward the kit. Control: Landing page for a $89 'Ten Minute Cut' bundle with identical layout, photography and price: cordless, quick-change blade, storage case, QR step-by-step guides, no professional-endorsement copy. Same $20 refundable deposit.
arguments.sample: About 30,000 US visitors over six weeks, roughly 15,000 per arm, recruited by paid social ads split evenly between the two page versions; the ads differ only in the four words naming the bundle. Cold prospects, no Andis customer list used.
arguments.measure: Deposit conversion rate (paid $20 deposits divided by unique visitors) per arm over six weeks, and the number and dollar value of deposits taken. Secondary: whether the buyer cuts their own hair or someone else's, to see who the mechanism applies to.

prediction_by_theory.T1: T1 predicts arm A (professional grade) converts at least 1.5 times arm B at the same $89 price, because the driver is confidence in a professional-looking result rather than saved time.
prediction_by_theory.T2: T2 predicts arm B (ten-minute bundle) converts at least 1.5 times arm A at the same $89 price, because the driver is saving time and salon trips rather than professional endorsement.

arguments.decision_rule: Combined conversion across both arms below 1.0% (fewer than about 300 deposits from 30,000 visitors) reads as home users refusing $89, roughly 1.5-3.5 times the $24.99-$59.99 kits Andis lists today (andis-athome-prices). At or above 1.0%, a winner is declared only if one arm converts at least 1.5 times the other with at least 150 deposits. Below 1.0% combined: no further at-home differentiation; next step is a bounded round of distributor conversations with the professional and groomer channel, no new product. Arm A wins by 1.5x with 150+ deposits: a 1,000-unit professional-grade home kit run at $89 with the same claim. Arm B wins by 1.5x with 150+ deposits: a 1,000-unit convenience bundle pilot. Neither arm ahead by 1.5x: price tolerance exists but the claim does not discriminate, so keep the current range and revisit assortment instead of a new line.

justification.learned: Reach is settled: Andis already sells an at-home line with kits at $24.99 and $59.99 (andis-athome-prices, andis-home-line), so further differentiation is the open question. Home cutting grew: 6 million joined with clippers and a 42% quarterly rise (andis-wahl-6-million), and a Wahl executive expected 10% more of the USA to cut at home (andis-wahl-10-percent). One account shows a $20 clipper lasting five cuts with a spouse cutting from videos (andis-attest-20-dollars), a warning for T1 and T2. No source shows willingness to pay above $59.99; support for T1 and T2 is company assertion, so premium demand is unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether anyone pays above the $24.99-$59.99 range Andis lists (andis-athome-prices). T1 and T2 both predict a premium but name different drivers; support is company assertion only (andis-home-line), so the buyer motive is untested. Rival explanations for any gap: ad wording, audience mix, novelty, deposit size. Andis margins are not public; test cost, sample and rates are my proposed parameters, not market facts.
justification.why_next: The test separates T1 from T2 because it holds price ($89) and page design constant and varies only the claimed benefit, so a conversion difference traces to the mechanism each theory names: T1 predicts the professional-grade arm wins because buyers want confidence in a professional result, T2 predicts the time-saving arm wins because buyers want to avoid salon trips. It also measures real commitment (paid deposits), not stated intent, and sets a floor: if combined deposit conversion is under 1.0% neither mechanism justifies a new at-home proposition, so every result leads to a bounded pilot run or to concentrating on the professional/groomer channel.
